FOREWORD This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Timber Sectional Committee had been approved by the Civil Engineering Division Council. Various Indian Standards have been formulated on different varieties on wooden furniture and cabinet making, namely, chairs, tables, almirahs, sofa sets etc. These specifications do not contain list of species to be used for the purpose, but refer to 1s 399 : 1963 Classification of commercial timbers and their zonal distribution ( revised)' for the same, which lists zonewise species for furniture and cabinets on the basis of general utilisation pattern in India and not on technical consideration for different furniture items. It also does not classify species for different types of furniture as the requirement of difl'erent type of furniture is different. Due to acute shortage of the traditionally accepted timber species and owing to the fact that characteristics of large number of species are now knowledge of properties and utilization available as a result of research carried out at Forest Research Institute, Dehra Dun, it was considered necessary to formulate a separate comprehensive standard on classification of Indian timbers for furniture and cabinets as has been done for door and window shutters and frames ( IS 12896 : 1990 Classification for Indian timbers for door and window shutters and frames' ). Requirements of timber for different types of furniture and cabinets are different. For example, for decorative and ornamental furniture, grain orientation, texture, colour and figure are important requirements. While for general utility furnitures these are not so essential. This classification is based on strength coefficient, weight, retention of shape, refractoriness to etc and seasoning, ease of working, grain, colour, texture, finish, polish, general appearance Classification and grading of Indian timbers for furniture and is adopted from the publication cabinet making' by S. S. Rajput and V. K. Gupta, Division of Forest Products, Forest Research Dehra Dun in the Journal of Timber Development Association ( India ), Vol 38, Institute, No. 1, 1992. This standard recommends 103 species in 4 groups and also lays down general requirement of quality of timber for furniture and cabinets.

Standard Mark

I

The use of the Standard Mark is governed by the provisions of the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder. The Standard Mark on products covered by an Indian Standard conveys the assurance that they have been produced to comply with the requirements of that standard under a well defined system of inspection, testing and quality control which is devised and supervised by BIS and operated by the producer. Standard marked products are also continuously checked by BIS for conformity to that standard as a further safeguard. Details of conditions under which a licence for the use of the Standard Mark may be granted to manufacturers or producers may be obtained from the Bureau of lndian Standards.

Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also revit,ved periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of `BIS Handbook. and `Standards Monthly Additions'.
